name: Zoroastrian Dari / Gabri / Gavruni / Behdini of Yazd
confidence_why: Ivanow 1935, the only description with an accent paragraph, calls the Gabri accent mobile, says it does not follow the Persian final-stress rule and puts it on the first syllable only in some verb forms, and Toosarvandani and Farudi 2003 independently report initial stress on verbs from their own Yazd fieldwork, so no source supports a fixed word-stress rule and none contradicts leaving the place…

catalog_quote: The accent is fairly mobile, and, as in many dialects, it does not observe the rule of LP of falling on the end of the word. The local Yazdi form of bazari has its own peculiarity, keeping the accent on the first, instead of the last syllable, which sounds rather odd, though the accent is never sharp. Gabri has the accent on the first syllable only in some verbal forms. The accent seems to consist neither in merely raising the voice, nor in merely prolonging it, but in doing both, in a varying degree, depending on intonation, and, perhaps, on the rate of speech. [Ivanow 1935: 48] ... [DLP 2003 Preliminary Report, Object Pronouns:] The first allomorph of each pair forms its own stress domain and for this reason it is believed to be a word, e.g. /'om 'ādēn/ 'give it to me!' (stress is always on the first syllable of the word). ... [DLP 2003 Summary of Findings p. 25-26:] One of the allomorphs, the “tonic” variant, forms its own stress domain; we can therefore analyze it as an independent word11, as opposed to a clitic12 or affix13 (stress in Dari is always on the first syllable of a verb): (5) óm ɑ́dεn 1SG:OBJP give:IMP:2SG ’give it to me!’ ... (7) m-e-t-ɑ́ 1SG:OBJP-CONT-give:PRES-3SG ‘he gives it to me’

new_statements.rule_in_words: The only explicit statement is a parenthetical: stress is 'always on the first syllable of a verb'. Taken literally this is fixed: initial syllable stress within the verb; but the source's own transcriptions put the accent on the verb STEM after the continuous prefix e- (e-vɛ́n-ɑ 'he throws', m-e-t-ɑ́ 'he gives'), so what is really described is stress on the (first syllable of the) verb stem, i.e. a morphological anchor. Nothing is said about nouns or other word classes. Tonic (syllabic) object and prepositional-object pronouns are independent words with their own stress (óm, mó, bíyo), the non-syllabic allomorphs are clitics inside the host's stress domain.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the parenthetical says 'always', but examples (7) m-e-t-ɑ́ and (8) e-vɛ́n-ɑ show stress off the verb-initial syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, verbs only; a fieldwork summary on the Qāsemābād village variety of Yazdi Dari (Yazd has ~30 village varieties per the same authors). Based on elicited forms and texts, 2003 fieldwork.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes the Qāsemābād village variety of Yazdi Zoroastrian Dari (Glottolog zoro1242, no separate dialect code); the authors note ~30 village varieties in Yazd plus a distinct Kermani dialect. Judeo-Yazdi (Jewish dialect of Yazd; Gindin 1998/2003, Lazard 1981, filed by Glottolog under zoro1242 refs but described by Gindin as mutually unintelligible with Gabri) has a separate, clearer statement in Encyclopaedia Iranica 'Yazd iv': 'As a rule, the stress is on the penultimate syllable' — do not merge it with the Zoroastrian variety.
